questions_and_answers.question_text: What does zhèi before an amount of time mean?
What is the usual Chinese order for "grandma and grandpa"?
What are the two meanings of shēntǐ?
What does hái mean before a state verb?
Write the Chinese for "We are going there in a couple of days."
What is a maternal grandmother called?
Write the Chinese for "You ought to straighten up your room."

answers.answer_text: Nǐ yīnggāi bǎ nǐde wūzi shōushi shōushi le.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "That restaurant isn't too bad."

articles.text:
3. A: Zhèi liǎngnián nǐ nǎinai      Has your grandmother's health been
      shēntǐ hǎo ma?                good the past couple of years?
   B: Hái hǎo, yǒu shíhou hái      Fairly good; sometimes she can still
      néng qǐlai shōushi shōushi    get up and straighten up the room.
      wūzi.

Notes on No. 3

zhèi liǎngnián: "the last couple of years." Zhèi before an amount of time often means "THE LAST" or "THE PAST." Liǎng does not necessarily mean exactly "two" but can mean "a couple," an INDEFINITE SMALL NUMBER.

Guò liǎngtian wǒmen jiu qù.      We are going there in a couple of days.

nǎinai: "paternal grandmother." For "grandma and grandpa," the Chinese order is almost always yéye nǎinai. (A maternal grandmother is called lǎolao or wàipó.)

(Northern)  lǎolao  lǎoyé   |  yéye    nǎinai
(Southern)  wàipó   wàigōng |  gōnggong  pópo
(Formal)    wàizǔmǔ wàizǔfù |  zǔfù     zǔmǔ
                            |  bàba     mā
                            |  fùqin    mǔqin

shēntǐ: "body" OR "health."

Bié zǒngshi pīnmìng niàn shū,    Don't always be knocking yourself out
děi duō zhùyì shēntǐ.            studying; you should look after your
                                 health more.

hái hǎo: "fairly good." You first learned hái as "still." When used BEFORE A STATE VERB, hái can also mean that the quality may STILL BE SAID TO APPLY, ALTHOUGH JUST BARELY. Often translated as "fairly, passably":

Zhèige diànyǐng hái bú cuò.      The movie was fairly good.
Nèige fànguǎnr hái kěyi.         That restaurant isn't too bad.

shōushi: "to straighten up"

Nǐ yīnggāi bǎ nǐde wūzi shōushi  You ought to straighten up your room.
shōushi le.

Shōushi xíngli means "to pack one's baggage."
